Subject: Denis, please stop the sale and call me

Denis,

I am writing in English so there is no misunderstanding, and so your wife can read this too. But I am writing to you, my brother, and I need you to answer me yourself.

I am furious. I have tried several times to write this, and every time I have had to stop because I do not want to say something I can never take back. But I cannot make this polite just to make it easier to read. What you have done has hurt me badly, and it puts my livelihood at risk.

On Thursday at six in the morning, I was in the bakery shaping baguettes when a photographer from the agency came into my shop. A stranger with a camera. That is how I learned you were putting Papa’s building on the market.

He told me that Mr. Denis had said I was okay with it.

I had not agreed to it. I did not even know about it. Karine had to calm me down in my own bakery while this man stood there, apparently expecting to take his pictures as if everything had already been discussed.

Afterward, I found the listing on Centris. Our building on rue Saint-Hubert, listed for $1,150,000. I had to go online to find out what was happening to the place where I have worked for thirty-one years.

Can you understand how humiliating that was? My employee was there. I had work to finish. And suddenly I was trying to understand something that you should have told me yourself, privately, before an agent or a photographer ever came through the door.

You live in Calgary, but you still have my telephone number. You could have called.

After Maman’s funeral, you told me, “No rush, we decide together.” I remember those words very clearly. Since she died in February, there has been enough to deal with already. When the estate was settled in August and the building became half yours and half mine, I believed we would do what you said. We would talk, look at the numbers, and decide together.

Together did not mean that I would discover your decision from a stranger at six in the morning.

I understand that your half of the building has value, and that you may want your money out. I am not asking you to pretend otherwise. You have your own life and your own needs. But I have needs too, and I have already put a serious proposal in front of you.

In September, on the telephone, I told you I wanted to buy your half. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. That was not an idle comment or a wish that I hoped would somehow work out. I had gone to the caisse because I was serious.

I know that $410,000 is not half of the asking price on that listing. There are numbers we need to discuss, and perhaps we will not agree immediately. But why did we not have that discussion? Why did you not tell me what you wanted, or explain why you thought my proposal would not work? You went ahead with an agent while I was still expecting a conversation with my brother.

I have paid $2,400 a month in rent to the estate and have never been late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 of my own money for the new roof. We need to discuss that too. It is a substantial amount, and it cannot simply be forgotten when we talk about the building and what each of us has put into it.

And please do not dismiss this as me being sentimental.

Of course I am sentimental about it. Papa bought that building in 1979. The bakery downstairs and the two apartments above are part of our family’s history. Do you remember how he let you sleep in the flour-sack room at the back when we were children? You loved being back there. I wonder if you remember that room when you look at the listing now.

But this is also a business. It is my work, my income, six employees, and thirty-one years of customers. People have been coming through that door for a large part of their lives. I cannot pick all of that up and move it somewhere else as if I am changing a mailing address.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. That is not far away. I do not know what a buyer would plan to do, and that uncertainty is exactly what frightens me. If a developer buys it, will they want to tear it down? Turn it into condos? Will I face rent I cannot possibly afford? If my rent doubles, the bakery cannot survive it.

You may see a sale as a way to settle your share. For me, it could mean losing the business I have spent thirty-one years building. I need you to take that seriously, even if you do not feel about the place the way I do.

What I am asking now is clear: take the building off the market this week and give us time to speak properly.

If you will not agree to take it off the market, then at the very least give me the first opportunity to buy your half before you make any commitment to someone else. Let us get the valuations, sit down with the figures, and find out whether we can reach a fair agreement. I am prepared to do that work promptly. I am not asking you to wait forever.

Until we have spoken, please do not send anyone else into the bakery for photographs or visits on the understanding that I have agreed. I have not. Whatever happens next needs to be discussed with me directly and arranged in advance.

I need a telephone call from you, not a text from your wife. I am not saying that to insult her or put her in the middle. She is welcome to read this and help you with the English. But this is between you and me, and I need to hear your voice and know that you have heard mine.

Please call me this week. I need to know whether you will stop the listing, and I need an honest explanation of why you went ahead without speaking to me.

I am very angry with you, Denis. I also do not want this to be how I lose my brother. We should be able to disagree about money without doing things behind each other’s backs. I still want us to find a way through this, but I cannot do that alone, and I cannot do it while the building is being sold out from under a conversation we never had.

Please stop and talk to me before this goes any further.
